records.sourceFile: Treatment after anterior cruciate ligament injury - Panther symposium ACL Treatment Consensus Group.pdf

paper.citation: Diermeier T, Rothrauff BB, Engebretsen L, Lynch AD, Ayeni OR, Paterno MV, et al. Treatment after anterior cruciate ligament injury: Panther Symposium ACL Treatment Consensus Group. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;8(6):2325967120931097.
paper.abstract: An international expert group used a modified Delphi process at the Panther Symposium 2019 to produce consensus statements on operative versus nonoperative treatment of ACL injury. Eleven of the 13 statements reached the 80% threshold in the abstract, and the recommendations address active patients by sport type, concomitant injury and instability.
paper.tldr: Experts agree that operative or nonoperative treatment can both be acceptable after ACL injury. Active patients who want to return to cutting and pivoting sports should be offered early anatomic reconstruction after a period of rehabilitation, while straight-plane athletes can be managed without surgery if they have no persistent instability.
paper.methods: A modified Delphi consensus. The symposium included experts from 18 countries, and the treatment working group had 34 participants, with 23 voting members. Statements were drafted from a literature review, circulated in an online survey, discussed at an in-person meeting and voted on by show of hands, with 80% agreement defined as consensus. Two liaisons, who did not vote, completed a MEDLINE review for each finalised statement.
paper.findings: Twelve statements were finalised. Nine were unanimous, and two reached strong consensus, including shared decision-making (82.6%) and the influence of anatomic differences (95.7%). Operative treatment was preferred for active patients who want to return to jumping, cutting and pivoting sports (100%). Nonoperative treatment was accepted for straight-plane activities (100%), with surgery indicated if instability persists in daily life (100%). The panel did not agree that delayed surgery is an option for temporary return to cutting and pivoting sport (43.4%).
paper.limitations: The authors state that most of the evidence is low-level, that few trials compare early surgery with rehabilitation and delayed surgery, and that data on concomitant meniscal or collateral ligament injury are limited. Of 13 statements discussed, 1 was removed for redundancy, so the 11 consensus statements are out of 12 finalised.
paper.practicalImplications: For active patients who want to return to jumping, cutting and pivoting sport, use shared decision-making and treat anatomic reconstruction as the preferred option, preceded by a period of progressive rehabilitation to resolve impairments. For straight-plane activities, structured progressive rehabilitation is an acceptable first option, with referral for reconstruction if instability or giving way persists. The panel did not reach consensus that delayed reconstruction is an option for a temporary return to cutting and pivoting sport, and the text links delay to more secondary meniscal and cartilage injury.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: this consensus offers no performance-enhancement guidance. Its relevance is to the return-to-sport decision for injured athletes, including the risk of secondary meniscal and cartilage injury when pivoting sport is resumed without surgery.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: this consensus can inform return-to-sport decisions after ACL injury. It supports shared decision-making, staged rehabilitation before reassessment, and anatomic reconstruction for athletes with persistent instability or those who want to return to cutting and pivoting sport. It does not give return-to-play clearance criteria or specific test thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Turf Toe Injuries in the Athlete - An updated review of treatment options, rehabilitation protocols, and return to play outcomes.pdf

paper.citation: Gupta A, Singh PK, Xu AL, Bronheim RS, McDaniel CM, Aiyer AA. Turf toe injuries in the athlete: an updated review of treatment options, rehabilitation protocols, and return-to-play outcomes. Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: This review summarises treatment modalities, rehabilitation protocols, return-to-play criteria and performance outcomes after turf toe (first metatarsophalangeal joint sprain) injuries in athletes.
paper.tldr: Fewer than 2% of turf toe injuries need surgery, and grade I and II injuries are managed non-operatively, while grade III injuries may need surgical repair and months of rehabilitation. Use the Anderson grade and the phased protocols to plan return, not a single fixed timeline.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the literature on classification, risk factors, imaging, non-operative and operative management, phased rehabilitation (Tables 4 and 5), return-to-play criteria and performance outcomes. No systematic search is described.
paper.findings: Under 2% of injuries require surgery, usually grade III injuries with MTP joint damage, bony injury or severe instability. Non-operative rehabilitation has three phases over up to 10 weeks, and operative rehabilitation four phases over up to 20 weeks. Grade I injuries usually return after 3 to 5 days, grade II injuries lose about 2 to 4 weeks, and grade III injuries lose 4 to 6 weeks or more. Median return after non-operative care was 5.85 weeks in one systematic review of 65 patients, against 14.7 weeks after surgery. About 70% of athletes with higher-grade injuries, treated either way, are expected to maintain their level of performance, and NFL studies found power ratings after return comparable to uninjured controls, though the authors say this may not hold for high-grade injuries.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, so its selection of sources is not reproducible. Many cited return-to-play figures come from small case series, retrospective league data and one systematic review with a wide time range (for example 6 to 156 weeks for surgery), and the authors note the performance effects in high-grade injuries are less certain. Table 1 gives grade II time loss as up to 2 weeks, while the abstract and conclusion give 2 to 4 weeks.
paper.practicalImplications: On the sideline, hold the player if any instability is found on examination, and image with weight-bearing radiographs to look for sesamoid migration. Start with rest, ice, compression and elevation for grade I and II injuries, use taping or a stiff-soled shoe on return, and restrict grade III athletes to straight-line running until they can sprint without pain before cutting drills.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: this review supports keeping push-off and cutting strength and range of motion at the centre of the rehabilitation phases, and it notes that after operative treatment performance may suffer in as many as 73% of athletes. Use the phased protocols to rebuild toe-off and cutting capacity before full practice.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review gives return-to-play criteria by grade, such as minimal pain with full weight-bearing, sprinting and cutting, and a 50 to 60 degree painless first MTP arc. These criteria come from composite sources, so use them as a checklist alongside examination, not as a standard clearance.

records.sourceFile: Updated return-to-play recommendations for collision athletes after cervical spine injury - A moified Delphi Consensus Study with the Cervical Spine Research Society.pdf

paper.citation: Schroeder GD, Canseco JA, Patel PD, Hilibrand AS, Kepler CK, Mirkovic SM, et al. Updated Return-to-Play Recommendations for Collision Athletes After Cervical Spine Injury: A Modified Delphi Consensus Study With the Cervical Spine Research Society. Neurosurgery. 2020.
paper.abstract: Previous return-to-play guidance for collision athletes after cervical spine injury has been limited by scant high-quality evidence and basic consensus methods. This modified Delphi study with spine surgeons and NFL team physicians produced consensus statements on return to play after cervical injury, stenosis, fusion and stinger episodes.
paper.tldr: A modified Delphi consensus of spine surgeons gives return-to-play statements for collision athletes after cervical injury, with strong agreement on several scenarios. Use it as expert consensus, not as proof of safety.
paper.methods: Modified Delphi study. A first-round online survey of 14 clinical scenarios and 38 questions went to CSRS members (48 responders). Thirteen statements were voted on at the 2019 CSRS meeting (95 voters). A third-round survey went to NFL-affiliated surgeons on 2-level ACDF clarification (8 responders). Consensus levels were defined by percent agreement.
paper.findings: Eight statements reached strong consensus, three weak consensus and two no consensus. After an episode of transient paralysis, strong consensus supported return to play for asymptomatic athletes with no T2 signal change and canal diameter above 10 mm (90.5%), and for those with resolved T2 change and canal diameter above 13 mm (81.25%). For a solid 1-/2-level ACDF with no T2 change, 84.4% agreed athletes could return while a 3-level ACDF should not. No consensus was reached for pseudarthrosis after ACDF (59.5%), and a 2-level ACDF split 50/50 in round 3. Strong consensus (84.5%) supported return after a stinger that resolves within 5 minutes.
paper.limitations: The authors list dependence on an expert panel, low neurosurgeon participation (6 of 48 round-1 respondents), inability to cover all cervical injuries and surgeries, and that results measure expert opinion only. Only 17 of 95 round-2 voters reported caring for professional collision athletes, and professional and nonprofessional physician responses did not differ significantly. The study did not set timelines for return to play.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the stenosis-based and fusion-based statements as a framework for discussing return-to-play with the spine team, and treat multi-level fusion and persistent MRI change as individual decisions that need specialist review.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable to training or performance programming. The statements concern medical clearance after cervical injury in collision sport.
paper.rtp: The paper is directly about return to play after cervical spine injury in collision athletes. Strong-consensus items (asymptomatic, no MRI T2 change, adequate canal diameter, solid 1-/2-level fusion) can inform the discussion, but the 2-level ACDF, pseudarthrosis and persistent MRI change scenarios are not settled and should not be used as clearance criteria without specialist input.

records.sourceFile: Uphill Walking Unveils Hidden Instability and Biomechanical Adaptations in Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Deficient Copers.pdf

paper.citation: Wang JY, Lu SH, Hu CH, Wu KW, Wang TM, Lu TW. Uphill Walking Unveils Hidden Instability and Biomechanical Adaptations in Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Deficient Copers. Gait Posture. 2025.
paper.abstract: Thirteen ACL-deficient copers and thirteen healthy adults walked up 3, 6 and 9 degree slopes with full-body motion capture and force plates. The ACLD group used a trunk anterior tilt strategy with altered knee forces and moments during uphill walking, which the authors interpret as functional instability hidden during level walking.
paper.tldr: ACL-deficient copers who looked normal on level walking leaned their trunk forward and shifted knee loading when walking uphill. Uphill walking may expose compensations that level-walking checks miss, but it has not been validated as a decision tool.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional matched-group gait laboratory study. Coper status required an MRI-confirmed complete unilateral ACL tear, 3 months to 5 years post-injury, with no level-walking impairment. Participants walked up a 3 m slope at 3, 6 and 9 degrees in a counterbalanced order while an eight-camera system and three force plates captured data for inverse dynamics. Two-way mixed ANOVA tested group (affected side, sound side, control) and slope effects.
paper.findings: Level walking moments did not differ between copers and controls. Uphill, the ACLD group had lower cadence than controls, and both knees showed greater anterior forces during initial double-limb and single-limb support and lower posterior forces at the end of single-limb support. The affected knee showed lower posterior force in terminal double-limb support, a greater anterior tibial angle, and a lower extensor moment at the end of single-limb support, alongside greater trunk anterior tilt, greater hip extensor moments at both hips and greater terminal double-limb dorsiflexion. Slope changed many variables in both groups, with no group by slope interactions.
paper.limitations: Instability was inferred, not measured: there was no EMG, fluoroscopy or record of giving way, and intersegmental resultants cannot separate muscle and ligament contributions. The Discussion calls the sample 'young ACLD copers' although Methods report a mean age of 41.8 +/- 12.6 years, and the abstract's description of knee force differences is narrower than the Results, which report them in both knees. Slopes were limited to 9 degrees, and the text is a Journal Pre-proof.
paper.practicalImplications: When screening ACL-deficient patients who appear to cope on level ground, adding a harder task such as uphill walking may reveal trunk and knee compensations. The authors' suggestion that this should inform surgical decisions is not tested in this study.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable to training programming. The sample is patients with untreated ACL deficiency, not athletes in training.
paper.rtp: Relevant background for assessing ACL-deficient copers: level-walking normality did not rule out uphill compensations. It cannot be used as a return-to-sport or surgical criterion, because the uphill pattern was not linked to giving way, reinjury or sport outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Use of Fantasy points in evaluating professional athlete performance after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Kajy M, Higginbotham DO, Etemad-Rezaie A, Ball GRS, Vaidya R. Use of Fantasy Points in Evaluating Professional Athlete Performance After Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Reconstruction. Cureus. 2023;15(3):e35855.
paper.abstract: Fantasy and wins above replacement (WAR) scores were calculated for 83 professional players who underwent ACL reconstruction in the NFL, NBA, NHL and MLB between 1992 and 2015. About half of players showed a decline in fantasy or WAR scores after surgery, and roughly a third regained their pre-injury level.
paper.tldr: Most professional players returned to play after ACL reconstruction, but about half had lower fantasy or WAR output afterward and only about a third regained their pre-injury level. The authors propose fantasy scores as a rough, objective performance marker for future work.
paper.methods: Descriptive cross-sectional study of professional players who missed at least one game for ACL reconstruction, identified from ESPN and league websites; players with repeat ACL surgery were excluded. Fantasy points and WAR were compiled from Rotoworld and FanGraphs, with pre-surgical level defined as the score in the year before surgery. Outcomes were return-to-play rate, career length after surgery, time to pre-surgical performance and recovery time, reported as counts, percentages and averages without statistical tests.
paper.findings: Fantasy or WAR scores fell after surgery in 13 of 25 NFL, 14 of 26 NBA, 8 of 17 NHL and 9 of 15 MLB players. The share who regained pre-injury performance was 36% (NFL), 42% (NBA), 35% (NHL) and 33% (MLB), taking 14 to 21 months on average. Reported return-to-play rates were 88% (NFL), 85% (NBA), 82% (NHL) and 93% (MLB). NFL players had the shortest average career after surgery (26 months) and NBA players the longest (64 months); average recovery time ranged from 8 months (NHL) to 13 months (NBA).
paper.limitations: Small male-only sample from public data, with no age-matched controls and no graft, concomitant injury or rehabilitation detail; undisclosed injuries may have affected performance. The abstract states 'Decreased fantasy scores ranged from 33% to 42%', but these values match Table 6's percentage of players reaching pre-injury performance, and no magnitude of score decline is reported. There are internal arithmetic inconsistencies (NHL return to play given as 11/17 = 82%; NFL percentages appear to use 26 rather than 25 as the denominator), and career length is underestimated for players active after 2015.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the results as descriptive context for the performance decline and return rates that follow ACL reconstruction in elite players. Do not use the fantasy-score decline as a clinical marker of graft success without a longitudinal, controlled analysis.
paper.athleteDev: Only about a third of players by league regained their pre-surgery fantasy or WAR level, which supports cautious expectations for performance recovery after ACL reconstruction. The paper does not test any training intervention.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return to play. Most players returned to professional play, but about half showed a decline in fantasy or WAR output afterward, and the paper cannot separate surgical, rehabilitation, injury and age effects.

records.sourceFile: Use of extracorporeal shockwave therapies for athletes and physically active individuals - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Rhim HC, Shin J, Kang J, Dyrek P, Crockett Z, Galido P, et al. Use of extracorporeal shockwave therapies for athletes and physically active individuals: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: The review examined the efficacy of extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) and outcomes for athletes and physically active individuals across 56 included studies. The authors found the strongest support for plantar fasciitis, lateral epicondylitis and proximal hamstring tendinopathy, and for adjunct use in medial tibial stress syndrome and osteitis pubis.
paper.tldr: ESWT looks effective alone for a few sports injuries and as an add-on to exercise for others, but most of the evidence is low level. Use it as one option to discuss with athletes, not as a general return-to-sport treatment.
paper.methods: The authors followed PRISMA and searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL and Web of Science in April 2023. They included RCTs, cohort, case-control, case series and case reports of ESWT in athletes, physically active adults and military cadets, and synthesised results narratively because the studies were too heterogeneous to pool.
paper.findings: Of 56 studies with 1874 participants, 18 were level I. Patellar tendinopathy was the most studied condition, with conflicting RCT results. Level I RCTs supported ESWT alone for plantar fasciitis, lateral epicondylitis and proximal hamstring tendinopathy, and ESWT added to exercise for medial tibial stress syndrome and osteitis pubis. Adverse events were mostly temporary pain and erythema, and were reported in 20 of 56 studies.
paper.limitations: No meta-analysis was possible, and 25 of the 56 studies were case series or reports, which the authors say should be interpreted with caution. Adverse-event reporting was incomplete, and only English-language studies were included.
paper.practicalImplications: Consider ESWT for plantar fasciitis, lateral epicondylitis and proximal hamstring tendinopathy, or as an add-on to exercise for medial tibial stress syndrome and osteitis pubis. For patellar tendinopathy, the authors call the benefit of adding ESWT to eccentric loading uncertain.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Outside bone-related injuries, most included studies let athletes keep training and competing as tolerated during ESWT, which may suit in-season athletes. Keep it inside a structured load plan, because the review found no clear advantage over exercise alone for patellar tendinopathy.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review reports return to sport in weeks to months, for example 16 of 20 professional athletes with proximal hamstring tendinopathy back at preinjury level by 3 months (mean 9 weeks) in one RCT with some concerns for bias. Other timings come from lower-level studies and should be treated as variable estimates. The review does not provide validated return-to-sport criteria after ESWT.

records.sourceFile: Using a Bayesian network to classify time to return to sport based on football injury epidemiological data.pdf

paper.citation: Yung KKY, Wu PPY, aus der Fünten K, Hecksteden A, Meyer T. Using a Bayesian network to classify time to return to sport based on football injury epidemiological data. PLoS ONE. 2025;20(3):e0314184.
paper.abstract: The authors built a discrete Bayesian network from public Bundesliga injury data (2014/15 to 2020/21) to classify days to return to sport and injury severity for individual players. Ten-fold cross-validation gave sensitivity of 0.24 to 0.97 for return-time categories and 0.73 to 1.00 for severity categories.
paper.tldr: A Bayesian network built from public Bundesliga injury data classified injury severity fairly well but return-to-sport timing less reliably, especially for mid-range durations. Treat it as a demonstration of decision support, not a validated prognosis tool.
paper.methods: This retrospective analysis of prospectively collected media-based injury data used 6143 time-loss injuries from 3374 Bundesliga player seasons. Twelve variables were included, with continuous ones manually discretised; the structure was partly fixed by expert knowledge and partly learned with a Bayesian search, parameters were fitted with EM, and performance was assessed with 10-fold cross-validation using sensitivity and user's accuracy.
paper.findings: Sensitivity for days to return to sport ranged from 0.24 (8 to 14 days) to 0.97 (under 3 days), with overall sensitivity of 0.66. Sensitivity for severity ranged from 0.73 (minimal) to 1.00 (severe), with overall sensitivity of 0.88. Type of injury and body region were the most influential variables for days to return, followed by age, contact status and training or match. In a hypothetical ankle sprain case, the network gave a 52% chance of return within 3 days.
paper.limitations: The model used only basic epidemiological variables, with no diagnosis, injury location detail or rehabilitation data, and was built on one league; injured players who did not return in the same season, and injuries with incomplete data, were excluded. The structure was partly set by the authors, and the text gives a minor inconsistency in severity sensitivity (0.73 to 1.00 in the results, 0.75 to 1.00 in the discussion). The case example is hypothetical and the authors call the study a pilot.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the network to explore how injury type, body region and age shift return-time distributions, and to build scenarios for team planning. Combine its output with clinical assessment, and do not use a single predicted day count as a return date.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Scenario analysis may help planners estimate how many players will be unavailable for training and matches across a season. The model cannot quantify the training load, match-readiness or performance effects needed for individual performance planning.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The network gives population-based probabilities of days to return that a clinician could use as a rough starting reference. It cannot establish an individual's readiness to return to play, because it lacks diagnosis, injury location and functional testing data.

records.sourceFile: Vertical jump impulse deficits persist from six to nine months after ACL reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Costley JAE, Miles JJ, King E, Daniels KAJ. Vertical jump impulse deficits persist from six to nine months after ACL reconstruction. Sports Biomechanics. 2021.
paper.abstract: The study aimed to evaluate countermovement jump phase-specific impulse and isokinetic strength inter-limb asymmetry from 6 to 9 months after ACL reconstruction in 44 male athletes, and to examine whether changes in strength asymmetry explained changes in impulse asymmetry. Strength asymmetry improved mainly through better performance of the reconstructed limb. Concentric impulse asymmetry reduced, while changes in strength asymmetry explained little of the impulse change. Graft type did not modulate the findings.
paper.tldr: Jump impulse and strength asymmetries are still present at 9 months after ACL reconstruction, though some improve. Strength gains alone do not explain the jump changes, so jump impulse deserves its own attention in late rehabilitation.
paper.methods: Forty-four male athletes with hamstring or bone-patellar tendon-bone autografts were tested 6 and 9 months after ACL reconstruction. Countermovement jump phase-specific impulse and knee isokinetic flexor and extensor strength were measured for both limbs. Two-way mixed-model ANOVAs compared sessions and graft types, and linear regression assessed the link between impulse and strength asymmetry changes.
paper.findings: Knee extension and flexion strength asymmetry improved from 6 to 9 months (extension ES -0.50; flexion ES -0.37), mainly through better performance of the ACL-reconstructed limb. The concentric CMJ impulse asymmetry fell significantly (ES -0.42), driven by a significant reduction in concentric impulse of the uninvolved limb, while eccentric deceleration impulse fell in both limbs and its asymmetry did not change. Change in extensor strength asymmetry explained only 12% of the change in eccentric deceleration impulse asymmetry and nothing else significantly, and patellar tendon graft athletes had larger extensor strength and CMJ impulse asymmetries than hamstring graft athletes at both time points.
paper.limitations: The design is observational with two time points and no control group, and post-operative rehabilitation was neither monitored nor controlled. Sport exposure increased between sessions, the hamstring graft group was 2.6 years older, and only a double-leg jump and vertical ground reaction force impulse (not joint loading) were assessed.
paper.practicalImplications: Check jump impulse in each limb, not just jump height or the asymmetry index, in later-stage rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction, because symmetry improved partly through decline in the uninvolved limb. Do not assume that improving knee strength asymmetry will fix jump impulse asymmetry.
paper.athleteDev: After ACL reconstruction, track jump impulse in both legs, not only the asymmetry ratio, since eccentric deceleration impulse fell in both limbs and concentric impulse fell in the uninvolved limb. Do not expect knee strength gains alone to correct jump impulse deficits.
paper.rtp: The paper shows that jump impulse and strength asymmetries persist at 9 months after ACL reconstruction and warns that using the uninvolved limb as the benchmark can overestimate the reconstructed limb's function. It supports including absolute jump impulse of both limbs in later-stage return-to-sport testing, but it does not set a passing threshold or show that these measures predict re-injury or return to sport.

records.sourceFile: When Is It Safe to Return to Sport After ACL Reconstruction Reviewing the Criteria.pdf

paper.citation: Kaplan Y, Witvrouw E. When Is It Safe to Return to Sport After ACL Reconstruction? Reviewing the Criteria. Sports Health. 2019.
paper.abstract: Review of return-to-sport criteria after ACL reconstruction. Five criteria were identified: psychological factors, performance and functional tests, strength tests, time, and modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors. Psychological readiness is a major factor; evidence for test validity is limited; delayed return beyond 9 months is suggested.
paper.tldr: Psychological readiness is a major factor in return-to-sport decisions after ACL reconstruction. Strength and hop tests are common but have little validation, and the authors suggest delaying return to beyond 9 months after surgery.
paper.methods: Electronic search of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBase, CINAHL and the Musculoskeletal Injuries Group register from inception to May 2018 (the text also says October 2018 in the abstract), using return to play or sport terms with guidelines, criteria and ACL reconstruction. Of 397 articles, 83 were reviewed after exclusions and duplicate removal.
paper.findings: Five criteria were identified. The authors cite a study in which 84% of patients were not ready to return to sport at 5.7 months, and a study in which only 5.6% of patients who passed RTS criteria before returning to level 1 sports were reinjured, compared with 37.5% of those who did not pass. They cite evidence that each month of delay before return up to 9 months reduced reinjury risk by 51%.
paper.limitations: Narrative synthesis of a mixed set of studies; the review does not grade evidence strength or report pooled estimates. The authors note that performance and functional test validity is largely unproven.
paper.practicalImplications: Psychological readiness should be assessed alongside physical tests before clearance. Staff should not treat a single test battery or the 90% limb symmetry rule as proof of readiness. The authors suggest RTS decisions after ACL reconstruction be delayed to at least 9 months, with extra caution for younger athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Movement quality during hop and landing tasks may matter as much as the hop score itself. Psychological readiness and fear of reinjury should be assessed alongside strength and performance testing.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper supports a multi-factor clearance process with psychological readiness, a test battery at discharge, and a preferred minimum of 9 months after surgery. The authors say the test-based criteria are not yet validated, so no single test should decide clearance alone.
